history.heading: Trading port
paragraphs: Kuwait, at the northern tip of the Persian Gulf, was settled in the early 18th century by clans from central Arabia. The Al Sabah family became rulers in 1752. Kuwait grew as a trading port, with dhow shipbuilding, pearl diving and caravan trade.
In 1899, seeking protection from the Ottomans, Kuwait signed an agreement with Britain, becoming a British protectorate.

history.heading: Oil and independence
paragraphs: Oil was discovered in 1938, and exports began after the Second World War, transforming Kuwait into one of the world's richest countries. It became independent on 19 June 1961.
On 2 August 1990 Iraq invaded and annexed Kuwait. A US-led coalition liberated the country in the 1991 Gulf War; retreating Iraqi forces set hundreds of oil wells on fire.

culture.heading: Society
paragraphs: Arabic is the official language, and English is widely used. Kuwaiti citizens are a minority of the population; most residents are foreign workers, mainly from South Asia, Egypt and the Philippines. Islam is the state religion; most citizens are Sunni with a significant Shia minority.
The diwaniya, a gathering of men in reception rooms, is central to social and political life. Machboos (spiced rice with meat) is a favourite dish. The Kuwait Towers are a national landmark.

politics.heading: Constitutional emirate
paragraphs: Kuwait is a constitutional emirate ruled by the Al Sabah family. Its elected National Assembly, established in 1963, has been the most powerful in the Gulf, able to question ministers. However, repeated clashes with governments led to frequent dissolutions, and in May 2024 the Emir suspended parliament and some constitutional articles for up to four years.
Kuwait has also revoked the citizenship of tens of thousands of people in recent years.

economy.heading: Oil wealth
paragraphs: Kuwait holds some of the world's largest oil reserves, and oil provides around 90 percent of government revenue. A large sovereign wealth fund, one of the oldest in the world, invests oil income abroad. Most citizens work in the public sector, and they enjoy free healthcare, education and generous subsidies.
Diversification has been slow. The Kuwaiti dinar is the world's highest-valued currency unit.
